To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

millennial-scale climate variations are only observed when ice volume is large and that the threshold of ice mass required for the occurrence of such variations has remained constant over the last 500,000 years.
millennial-scale climate variations during the past 500 kyr were linked to the continental ice mass and were only observed if continental ice mass exceeded a threshold value.

the sediment-color record from core MD01-2442 shows a distinct millennial-scale signal during the last 500,000 years, that this signal is linked to the size of the continental ice mass, and that this signal is only detectable if the continental ice mass exceeds the threshold level equivalent to sea level lowering of about 40% during the last glaical maximum.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of millennial-scale climate change during the last 500,000 years, with a focus on the interplay between continental ice mass and climate variability.
the reconstruction of late Pleistence climate variability on millenial time scales.
the question whether the occurrence of millennial-scale climate fluctuations is related to the size of continental ice mass and the associated sea level lowering.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the millennial-scale climate variations during the past 500 ka were driven by the interaction between ice sheet dynamics and oceanic processes, and the strength of this interaction was modulated by changes in the global ice volume.
large-amplitude millenial-scale climate variability was a characteristic feature of late Pleistocence climate only if continental ice sheets were sufficiently large to lower sea level by 40% or more.
the threshold level for millennial-scale climate instability was reached during the last glaciations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the millennial climate variability during the late Pleistocene was not a permanent feature of the climate system but was rather a consequence of the presence of a large continental ice sheet.
the climate system has the ability to generate millennial-scale climate variations, but the occurrence of these variations is controlled by the state of the continental ice mass.
the climate system is more sensitive to external forcing if ice sheets are large.
The main takeaway from our work is that
millennial-scale climate oscillations are not a constant feature of the climate system, but rather occur only when a certain threshold level of ice mass is exceeded.
the amplitude of millennial-scale climate fluctuations is not a constant feature of the late Pleistocene but is rather dependent on the state of the continental ice sheets.
millennial-scale climate oscillations were only pronounced when continental ice sheets were sufficiently large to provide a source of ice-rafted debris for the ocean.
